cards.title: Streaming space for additive \(L_\infty\) estimation
cards.formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors, the optimal worst-case bit space for a one-pass randomized streaming algorithm that returns only an estimate \(z\) of \(\|f\|_\infty\), with \[\Pr\!\left[|z-\|f\|_\infty|\le\frac{\|f\|_p}{k}\right]\ge\frac23.\] The bound must describe its dependence on domain size \(n\ge2\), update budget \(M\ge2\), accuracy parameter \(k\ge4\), norm flag \(p\in\{1,2\}\), and update mode \(b\in\{\mathrm{insert},\mathrm{difference}\}\), in the model below.
cards.why: Separate the memory needed for one largest-magnitude estimate from the information needed to identify heavy coordinates, while accounting for error scale, domain size and cancellation.
cards.status_note: Partially resolved historical source direction. The PODS 2016 paper explicitly reports an answer for insertion-only L1-relative maximum-frequency estimation, so that endpoint is not advertised here as a fresh open problem. The present full space characterization retains both source norms and update modes with explicit editorial conventions. Its complete current status was not established by the bounded 14 September 2026 search; source proofs were not independently verified.

progress.text: Cormode asks for reduced bit space for scalar \(L_\infty\) estimates under \(L_1\)- or \(L_2\)-scaled additive error, discussing insertions and differences of streams.

Bhattacharyya–Dey–Woodruff report improved maximum-frequency space and a resolution of the insertion-only \(L_1\) variant in their formulation. This is a partial resolution of the broader source direction.

sentences: The output is a single estimate of the largest absolute coordinate of a streamed frequency vector.
The allowed additive error is one over k times the final L1 or L2 norm.
Insertion-only streams and signed differences of two streams are distinct modes of the same resource question.
The target is a tight bit-space characterization in the domain size, update budget and accuracy.
A 2016 paper reports resolving the insertion-only L1 part, while this review does not certify a complete characterization of all cases.

cards.definitions: Parameters \(n,M,k\) are integers supplied in binary before the stream, together with the two flags. The frequency vector starts at \(f=0\in\mathbb Z^n\). There are at most \(M\) updates \((i,\Delta)\), where \(1\le i\le n\). In insert mode every \(\Delta=1\); in difference mode \(\Delta\in\{-1,1\}\), and update \((i,\Delta)\) replaces \(f_i\) by \(f_i+\Delta\). Negative intermediate and final frequencies are allowed in difference mode. Equivalently, positively and negatively tagged insertions describe the difference of two streams, with their combined length bounded by \(M\). Only this bound, not the actual stream length, is known in advance. Set \(\|f\|_1=\sum_i|f_i|\), \(\|f\|_2=(\sum_i f_i^2)^{1/2}\), and \(\|f\|_\infty=\max_i|f_i|\). The additive tolerance is scaled by the final vector, not by the total number of updates; cancellation therefore matters. At the end, output one rational number \(z\) as a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator. No coordinate identity or list of heavy items is requested. On \(f=0\), the success event requires exactly \(z=0\). The fixed stream is chosen independently of the algorithm’s private independent fair random bits. There is one terminal query, with success at least \(2/3\) separately on every valid stream; there is no requirement of simultaneous success at all prefixes. Use a uniform randomized multitape streaming machine with one fixed finite program for all parameters, no advice, no public random table and no oracle. The parameter header is read-only. An update is available in a read-only buffer until the machine advances to the next update, after which earlier updates cannot be revisited. Every work-tape bit, stored random bit or seed, counter, index, table and input-dependent retained state counts toward space, including all scratch space used during processing and final decoding. Input and write-only output cells do not count; copies do. Address and head-position information accessible to the algorithm that can carry input-dependent state is charged. The unreadable physical position of the one-way stream is not work memory; the number of updates already consumed is not supplied as a free clock. Random bits cannot be reread unless retained. The machine must halt on every valid finite stream and every random tape; computation time is unrestricted. Space is the maximum number of charged bits over all such streams and random tapes for the given parameters, not its expectation. Bounds may be piecewise over parameter regimes and must use ordinary asymptotic notation with all logarithmic factors exposed. The reciprocal-integer accuracy convention \(\epsilon=1/k\), finite update budget, private randomness and bit accounting make the source’s qualitative space question precise.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a tight asymptotic space characterization across the complete parameter domain and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean. It must include uniform algorithms attaining the stated upper bounds, their terminal-error and worst-case-space guarantees, and matching lower bounds for every algorithm in the same model, up to constants independent of all parameters and flags. A one-sided bound, a bound only for identifying heavy items, a word count hiding bit costs, or a result for only one norm or update mode does not determine the whole characterization. This is an asymptotic resource target: the benchmark does not apply an additive 1/100 tolerance to big-O or big-Theta bounds.

context_blocks.text: The largest absolute frequency is a scalar statistic. Identifying which item attains it can require additional information about a large item domain. The source asks whether that distinction can reduce memory when an additive error measured against the full frequency vector is allowed.

The two norms specify different accuracy requirements. For \(f=(3,-2,0)\), the target value is three, while the error scale is either \(5/k\) or \(\sqrt{13}/k\). For a difference stream, many updates can cancel, so an error proportional to the number of processed updates can be much larger than the permitted error.

This card retains both error scales and both update settings from the source as flags in one space-complexity characterization. It asks for their full dependence on the domain, stream budget and accuracy, rather than for a new yes/no claim that every historical bound remains unimproved. The exact finite-input and randomness conventions are editorial specifications.

Bhattacharyya, Dey and Woodruff explicitly report answering the insertion-only \(L_1\)-error part of the 2006 question. For maximum-frequency estimation they report \(O(\epsilon^{-1}\log\epsilon^{-1}+\log n+\log\log t)\) bits, where \(t\) is the stream length, and describe optimality in their stated regimes. Their result is recorded as existing progress, not as an unsolved insertion-only endpoint.

That result does not by itself supply the \(L_2\)-relative or signed-difference cases. In particular, insertion-only \(\|f\|_1\) equals the number of updates, whereas cancellation destroys that equality in a difference stream. A theorem’s norm, update promise, scalar versus item output, and parameter restrictions must all match before it can be counted toward the full target.

The original page explicitly distinguishes bit space from a count of machine words: random-function descriptions and counters also consume memory. The reviewed card preserves that distinction. The requested comparison is therefore about complete memory usage, not only the number of stored counters.

A full characterization would identify which memory costs arise from maintaining frequency magnitudes and which arise from recovering item names. It would clarify the value of scalar summaries for comparing streams over large domains and the cost of allowing deletions or cancellation.

cards.title: Conforti–Cornuéjols conjecture
cards.formal: Does every finite clutter with the packing property have the max-flow min-cut property? Equivalently, if every deletion/contraction minor satisfies unweighted integral packing–covering equality, must weighted integral packing–covering equality hold for every nonnegative integer weight vector?
cards.definitions:
A clutter \(\mathcal C\) on a finite ground set \(E\) is a family of subsets of \(E\), no one properly containing another. Its original members are nonempty; the empty family is allowed. A cover is a set \(T\subseteq E\) meeting every member, and \(	au(\mathcal C)\) is its minimum cardinality. A packing is a family of pairwise disjoint members; \(
u(\mathcal C)\) is its maximum cardinality. Deleting an element removes it from the ground set and discards all members containing it. Contracting an element removes it from the ground set and from every member, then keeps only inclusion-minimal members. A minor is obtained by any finite sequence of these operations, including the empty sequence. The packing property is \(	au(\mathcal D)=
u(\mathcal D)\) for every minor \(\mathcal D\). For the empty family both numbers are zero. For the degenerate minor \(\{\varnothing\}\), set both numbers to \(+\infty\): no cover exists and arbitrarily many copies of the empty member can be packed. These conventions give no obstruction from degenerate minors. For an original clutter and capacities \(w\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{E}\), define \[	au_w(\mathcal C)=\min\left\{\sum_{e\in T}w_e:T\subseteq E	ext{ is a cover}ight\},\qquad 
u_w(\mathcal C)=\max\left\{\sum_{F\in\mathcal C}y_F:y\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{\mathcal C},\ \sum_{F
i e}y_F\le w_e	ext{ for every }e\in Eight\}.\] Multiplicities \(y_F\) allow repeated packed members, and every copy consumes one unit of capacity at each of its elements. Both optima are finite because original members are nonempty. The max-flow min-cut (MFMC) property is equality of these optima for every nonnegative integer capacity vector; the weights and ground-set size have no fixed upper bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal implication, or of its logical negation. An affirmative answer must establish \(\tau_w(\mathcal C)=\nu_w(\mathcal C)\) for every clutter with the packing property and every nonnegative integer vector \(w\). A negative answer must exhibit a finite clutter and such a vector with \(\tau_w(\mathcal C)>\nu_w(\mathcal C)\), and verify the packing property for every minor. A finite census, a proper subclass theorem, or fractional duality alone is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: Packing and covering often give two descriptions of the same combinatorial optimum. In a clutter, the unweighted equality can fail. Requiring equality after every deletion and contraction removes many such obstructions. The Conforti–Cornuéjols conjecture asks whether this local robustness already guarantees equality for every integer capacity vector.

For a concrete example, take E as the vertices of a bipartite graph and the clutter members as its edges. Covers are vertex covers and packings are matchings. This illustrates the familiar kind of min–max equality that the general conjecture seeks to characterize, without restricting its input to graph edge families.

For the member-by-element incidence matrix \(A\), whose entry \(A_{F,e}\) is one precisely when \(e\in F\), the corresponding fractional problems are \(\min\{w^{\mathsf T}z:Az\ge\mathbf1,\ z\ge0\}\) and \(\max\{\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y\le w,\ y\ge0\}\). The conjectured equality concerns integer solutions, and hence is stronger than ordinary linear-programming duality. It asks for integral optima on both sides for every integer weight.

Schrijver’s Survey Question 68 calls the target the assertion that every packing hypergraph is Mengerian. The terminology differs, but its packing property includes all minors and its conclusion includes arbitrary nonnegative integer weights. Checking only the all-ones weight on the original instance would yield a much weaker, insufficient hypothesis.

Abdi and Schwarcz’s July 2026 manuscript calls the statement the replication conjecture and explicitly retains it as open. It reports verification for clutters on at most ten elements and for a specified bounded-degree family of cuboids. These are finite or restricted confirmations, not a proof for arbitrary ground-set size.

The same work gives a finite set of weight vectors sufficient to test the MFMC property of a fixed clutter, with an improved bound on their entries. This makes checking individual instances more effective. The number and size of possible clutters still grow without bound, so instance-wise testability does not prove the universal implication.

Roy and Saha report a proof for \((n-2)\)-uniform clutters: every member has size exactly \(n-2\) when the ground set has \(n\) elements. Arbitrary clutters can have unrelated member sizes, so this subclass result leaves the stated universal implication unchanged.

cards.why: Identify whether all obstructions to weighted integral packing–covering duality are already visible as unweighted failures in minors, a central issue in integer programming and combinatorial optimization.

importance.reason: A central conjecture connecting minor obstructions, integral linear programming and packing–covering duality. Schrijver treats it as a major survey question, and a July 2026 primary paper develops both theoretical and computational methods around it.

cards.title: Polynomial-time mixed equilibria in coordination polymatrix games
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: Is there a uniform deterministic algorithm that, for every finite rational coordination-only polymatrix game, outputs an exact mixed Nash equilibrium in time polynomial in the complete binary input length?
cards.why: Locate the tractability boundary for exact mixed equilibrium when every pairwise interaction has common payoffs, distinguishing the complexity of network coordination from general games and from pure local-search equilibria.
cards.status_note: The exact coordination-only tractability question is open in the checked primary sources. A bounded later-work search on 14 September 2026 found no matching resolution. Pure-equilibrium hardness and the 2025 two-team result concern different tasks; they are not treated as a refutation or an unconditional lower bound for this proposition.

progress.text: Cai–Daskalakis establish pure-equilibrium PLS-completeness and mixed-equilibrium membership in PLS and PPAD, leaving polynomial-time mixed-equilibrium tractability open.
Savani poses the coordination-only mixed-equilibrium complexity question in the Dagstuhl report.
The two-team hardness result allows zero-sum interactions between teams and hence does not settle this coordination-only restriction.

sentences: Each player uses one action across several pairwise interactions in a graph.
The two endpoints of each edge receive equal payoffs from that interaction.
The target is a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm returning any exact mixed Nash equilibrium.
Pure equilibria are permitted outputs, but an algorithm may also use genuinely mixed profiles.
Known pure-equilibrium and adversarial two-team hardness results do not settle this coordination-only mixed search task.

cards.definitions: An instance is a finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), with \(V=\{1,\ldots,r\}\), and for each player \(i\) a nonempty explicitly enumerated action set \(A_i=\{1,\ldots,k_i\}\). Each edge \(\{i,j\}\), with \(i<j\), carries an explicitly listed matrix \(M_{ij}\in\mathbb Q^{k_i\times k_j}\). If its endpoints choose \(a\in A_i\) and \(b\in A_j\), both receive the same edge payoff \(M_{ij}(a,b)\). Set \(M_{ji}(b,a)=M_{ij}(a,b)\) for reverse orientation. Each player selects one action for all its incident edges and receives the sum of those edge payoffs; nonedges contribute zero. A mixed profile \(p=(p_i)_{i\in V}\) uses independent probability vectors \(p_i\) on \(A_i\). For a pure deviation \(a\in A_i\), write \[v_i(a,p_{-i})=\sum_{j:\{i,j\}\in E}\sum_{b\in A_j}p_j(b)M_{ij}(a,b),\qquad u_i(p)=\sum_{a\in A_i}p_i(a)v_i(a,p_{-i}).\] It is an exact Nash equilibrium when \(v_i(a,p_{-i})\le u_i(p)\) for every player \(i\) and every action \(a\). The required output explicitly lists nonnegative rational probabilities summing to one for each player. A pure profile is allowed as a degenerate mixed profile; neither full support nor a genuinely randomizing player is required. Vertices, edges and all actions are listed, and each payoff is encoded by a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator with delimiters. Thus the input length \(N\) includes the action lists, graph and every payoff bit; no succinct payoff circuit is allowed. Use a uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program, no advice or oracles, and a bound \(C(N+1)^d\) on all valid inputs for constants \(C,d\) independent of the instance. Charge every bit operation and output bit. The target is exact equilibrium, with no approximation parameter or promise on payoff magnitudes, graph degree or action counts.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of the stated uniform polynomial-time algorithm, including termination, the full bit bound and exact equilibrium correctness, or of its logical negation. A hardness reduction under an unproved separation establishes only a conditional conclusion. A polynomial bound in numerical payoff magnitudes, a fixed graph or action-count special case, or an approximate-equilibrium algorithm without an exact guarantee does not meet the target.

context_blocks.text: Coordination is imposed locally: the two endpoints agree on the payoff of their shared interaction. A player with several neighbors must nevertheless choose one action that participates in all those interactions. Equal payoffs on each edge therefore do not mean that every player has the same total payoff on every full profile.

For example, on a three-vertex path, the middle player receives the sum from both edges, while each endpoint receives only its single edge payoff. The middle player can face conflicting preferences from its two interactions even though each separate interaction gives identical rewards to its two participants.

The 2014 Dagstuhl report attributes the network-coordination question to Rahul Savani and explicitly imposes equality in each edge’s payoff pair. The present card makes polynomial-time tractability the binary target of that broader complexity question; Cai and Daskalakis already explicitly ask whether this search problem is in P.

Cai and Daskalakis show that finding a pure equilibrium is complete for polynomial local search, abbreviated PLS, while finding any mixed equilibrium belongs to both PLS and the parity-based total-search class PPAD. Permitting mixed output changes the search task even though pure equilibria exist: hardness of finding a pure equilibrium alone does not classify the task that may return any mixed one.

The same primary source records that rational polymatrix games have mixed equilibria with rational probabilities and polynomial description length. Exact output is consequently meaningful in the bit model and is not obstructed by a need to print arbitrary irrational numbers.

Hollender, Maystre and Nagarajan prove hardness for two-team polymatrix games with coordination inside teams and zero-sum interactions between teams. Their result allows adversarial edges absent from this card, and therefore does not classify coordination-only games. Likewise, an equilibrium constrained to be symmetric is a different output requirement.

The question tests whether permitting players to randomize makes arbitrary networks of local common-interest interactions computationally tractable. The input restriction and the freedom to return any equilibrium both matter; neither general-game hardness nor the ease of a single two-player coordination game settles this network case.

cards.context:
Coordination is imposed locally: the two endpoints agree on the payoff of their shared interaction. A player with several neighbors must nevertheless choose one action that participates in all those interactions. Equal payoffs on each edge therefore do not mean that every player has the same total payoff on every full profile.

For example, on a three-vertex path, the middle player receives the sum from both edges, while each endpoint receives only its single edge payoff. The middle player can face conflicting preferences from its two interactions even though each separate interaction gives identical rewards to its two participants.

The 2014 Dagstuhl report attributes the network-coordination question to Rahul Savani and explicitly imposes equality in each edge’s payoff pair. The present card makes polynomial-time tractability the binary target of that broader complexity question; Cai and Daskalakis already explicitly ask whether this search problem is in P.

Cai and Daskalakis show that finding a pure equilibrium is complete for polynomial local search, abbreviated PLS, while finding any mixed equilibrium belongs to both PLS and the parity-based total-search class PPAD. Permitting mixed output changes the search task even though pure equilibria exist: hardness of finding a pure equilibrium alone does not classify the task that may return any mixed one.

The same primary source records that rational polymatrix games have mixed equilibria with rational probabilities and polynomial description length. Exact output is consequently meaningful in the bit model and is not obstructed by a need to print arbitrary irrational numbers.

Hollender, Maystre and Nagarajan prove hardness for two-team polymatrix games with coordination inside teams and zero-sum interactions between teams. Their result allows adversarial edges absent from this card, and therefore does not classify coordination-only games. Likewise, an equilibrium constrained to be symmetric is a different output requirement.

The question tests whether permitting players to randomize makes arbitrary networks of local common-interest interactions computationally tractable. The input restriction and the freedom to return any equilibrium both matter; neither general-game hardness nor the ease of a single two-player coordination game settles this network case.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Inactive records are archived outside the catalogue, exports and editorial work. Their content, stable IDs and reasons are retained; imports cannot reactivate them. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Inactive cards, including resolved records, are archived outside the ranking without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.

benchmark_selection.basis: Individual editorial review of saved titles, importance rationales, problem statements, source notes and working summaries. This is a review of importance and topical diversity, not a fresh verification of open status or completion of draft formulations. Importance scores are preserved.
